sources.originalTitle: yes, you should move to san francisco
sources.summary: Hubert Thieblot, founder of Founders Inc and ex-Curse founder, makes the case for moving to SF and explains the campus, programs and investment model. He argues proximity to ambitious peers raises ambition, and that working side by side beats pitch decks as a way to invest.

principles.text: Being in San Francisco changes a founder's trajectory and ambition; nothing feels impossible.
principles.quote: The trajectory of my company completely [music] changed. I became way more ambitious and nothing felt impossible.

principles.text: Founders should spend most of their time in a tight build, learn, iterate loop alongside other founders.
principles.quote: There's only one thing that matters here. Building, learning, and iterating. 90% of your experience will be [music] hitting this cycle every day with other founders on campus.

principles.text: Skip pitch decks; judge potential by working with founders in person, and let founders judge the investors too.
principles.quote: We absolutely hate pitch decks. We never liked making them as founders because [music] building a company is about doing, not making a polished presentation.

principles.text: Learn from founders a few steps ahead of you via office hours and sessions.
principles.quote: Our team hosts regular office [music] hours and sessions with experienced founders who can be one or 100 steps ahead of where you are right now.

principles.text: Invest only after a trial period of real collaboration where both sides feel acceleration.
principles.quote: you apply online, we invite you to our space, work closely with you to accelerate your growth, and if we both feel that there's a good fit, we [music] invest in your startup.

principles.text: Back physical AI and robotics founders early, betting they become the biggest companies.
principles.quote: We envision a future where physical AI and robotics are the biggest companies in the world.

sources.title: How Curse built a gamer platform: community-made apps, ads plus premium, employees who play
sources.originalTitle: CBS5 Interview with Curse, Inc. CEO Hubert Thieblot
sources.summary: A 2010 CBS5 interview where Hubert Thieblot explains Curse, a platform for World of Warcraft and MMO players. He covers being a distribution platform for community-built tools, a two-channel revenue model of ads and subscriptions, and staffing with real gamers.

principles.text: Be the distribution platform and let the community build the product; you host and distribute.
principles.quote: we don't do them it's actually the community doing them so we are just a distribution platform

principles.text: Run two revenue channels: advertising for the free audience, plus a subscription for premium features.
principles.quote: we have two Revenue channel the first one is obviously advertising

principles.text: Put your sales team where your traffic is: Curse moved to the US because 45% of its traffic was there.
principles.quote: we have 45% of our traffic in the US so we had to have our sales team here

principles.text: In a fast-moving industry, stay relevant by hiring people who live the product and play every game themselves.
principles.quote: I think it's really important to play all the games to know what's going on

principles.text: Hire team members who are your own customers; they know exactly what users want and need.
principles.quote: these are Gamers that are providing a service for other Gamers they know exactly what they want and need

principles.text: Assume what you build today will be obsolete soon and keep reinventing the product.
principles.quote: what we were doing at this time were would be completely nearly useless now

sources.title: Curse CEO on launching Curse Voice: fixing real player pain, platform strategy, free-first monetization
sources.originalTitle: Curse CEO Hubert Thieblot on Curse Voice - controversy, future development, and more
sources.summary: Hubert Thieblot explains how Curse built a free voice and overlay app for League of Legends by fixing the questions players keep asking in chat. He covers handling publisher risk through transparency, scaling cheaply with better compression, delaying monetization to win 100M PC gamers, and shifting from content to technology platforms.

principles.text: Build features from the questions users repeatedly ask; fix friction that stops them from doing the real thing.
principles.quote: what are the things that people ask all the time in chat and it's like when is your old app up when is dragon when is baron these are like the three main things people ask for so we were like okay well we'll fix it

principles.text: Focus on improving quality of life, not building an all-in-one tool that does everything for the user.
principles.quote: our goal is not to have like the ultimate timer application that does everything for you. That's not what we want to do. Uh, our goal is to improve quality of life of the players and improve communications.

principles.text: Be transparent with the platform owner early and stay open to their concerns, while weighing what your user base wants.
principles.quote: we didn't build this you know uh hoping that you know uh this would be a big surprise for anyone in the future. We've actually been in beta uh for about three months now.

principles.text: Make the core service free, push monetization out, and prioritize reaching the whole addressable audience first.
principles.quote: monetization is not is not my worry. Um, right now our number one objective is there is about 100 million hardcore PC gamer outside of China. I want to get all of them on our voice platform.

principles.text: Fix stability first; a crash or FPS hit kills trust in a tool that runs inside someone's game.
principles.quote: We don't want to crash your game. We want we don't want to impact your FPS.

principles.text: Technology scales worldwide faster than content, so move toward platform and technology businesses.
principles.quote: we see the technology aspect as uh easier to scale and to grow worldwide because um content has more local than uh uh technology

sources.title: How Hubert Thieblot picks founders: ambition, speed and technical depth over the idea
sources.originalTitle: The VC Who Writes $150K Checks on Vibes - Hubert Thieblot, Curse Founder | Due Diligence Ep. 4
sources.summary: In a comedic interview, Hubert Thieblot explains how he writes early checks on vibe, backing ambitious, fast-moving technical founders instead of judging the idea. He also shares founder advice: pick the hardest problem you care about, and don't hire a compliance officer too early.

principles.text: Early-stage investing is mostly about the founder's vibe, not a heavy diligence process.
principles.quote: I think you're going to think it's weird, but I mostly invest on vibe.

principles.text: Judge founders on ambition, speed at unblocking themselves, and ability to build something technically hard. The idea matters little.
principles.quote: Are you going to move really fast and find ways to unblock yourself? I know that's hard to hear for you, but and then how technical are you?

principles.text: Ask for the idea to gauge ambition, not to evaluate the idea itself.
principles.quote: generally I ask the idea because I want to know your ambitions. But I actually don't care too much about the idea.

principles.text: Dream big and pick the hardest problem you genuinely care about, because passion carries you through the hard moments.
principles.quote: you as a founder should dream the biggest you can and go for the hardest problem to work on that you also actually care about.

principles.text: Founders working on things they don't care about quit the first time it gets really hard.
principles.quote: it's very obvious when people just work on random things that they don't care about.

principles.text: Don't add compliance overhead before you actually need it; speed comes first.
principles.quote: Do not hire a compliance officer before you have something that needs a compliance officer.

sources.title: How Curse Inc. chose Huntsville, Alabama over Silicon Valley to solve its hiring bottleneck
sources.originalTitle: Curse Inc. CEO: Why our tech firm moved its headquarters to Alabama
sources.summary: Hubert Thieblot explains why Curse moved HQ from San Francisco to Huntsville. Hiring was the biggest growth constraint, and competing with well-funded Bay Area companies for talent was not a game worth playing. He walks through the five criteria used to pick a city and the logic of being a big fish in a smaller, rising market.

principles.text: As a company scales, growing the team fast enough becomes the biggest challenge, so design your location and strategy around talent.
principles.quote: As we have grown, the biggest challenge we face is to grow our team to keep up with our company.

principles.text: Don't fight much larger, better-funded rivals head-on for talent; pick a different battlefield.
principles.quote: we looked at the environment surrounding talent and decided we couldn’t just “slug it out” with the very large and very well-funded companies that exist in San Francisco

principles.text: Evaluate HQ location on explicit criteria: talent pool, work-life balance, business environment, cost efficiency, and potential.
principles.quote: The factors that were most important to us were the following;

principles.text: Look for a talent market with real depth but not so much competition that hiring becomes slow and prohibitively expensive.
principles.quote: We needed a location with a strong tech presence but not so much that competition would make securing employees prohibitively expensive or take so long that it slows down our production.

principles.text: Optimize for value per dollar, not simply the cheapest option; saving money alone isn't the goal.
principles.quote: the key isn’t to simply save. We could put a team in another country for that. Rather, we wanted to get the most bang for our buck

principles.text: Skip the trendy default and be an early, important part of a rising ecosystem rather than a drop in the bucket in a big one.
principles.quote: Curse would rather blaze a trail toward an up and coming community and be a part of its evolution from the very beginning.

sources.title: How Curse grew from a WoW add-on database to a funded MMO portal (2007 Q&A)
sources.originalTitle: Q&A: Curse's Thieblot & Kriegel On Social MMO Networks
sources.summary: Hubert Thieblot explains how Curse started as a guild website and WoW add-on database, grew by being the first, biggest and best in its niche, then added social tools years later. He covers moving to San Francisco, raising a $5M Series A, and expanding toward publishers and premium subscriptions.

principles.text: Build the tool you personally need as a user; that is how the business started.
principles.quote: it was a complete mess to try and get information on add-ons and updates from the official forums and all the people posting on the website. So I decided to make a database

principles.text: Being first, biggest and best in one useful niche (add-ons) drives traffic long before you add features.
principles.quote: we were the first, the biggest and the best on the net. We basically have been surfing on that wave for two years and a half

principles.text: Start small with no grand plan; a personal, ad-funded site can turn into a real business once traction shows.
principles.quote: I just wanted it to be a personal business where I could live off of advertising. I would never have expected it to be this big, two years later.

principles.text: Move to where your competitors and talent are, and aim to innovate instead of copying a US concept.
principles.quote: We don’t want to be a copycat – taking a US concept and bringing it to Europe. We want to be innovative, and we want to compete against IGN, GameSpot and all the other big players.

principles.text: Social networks need a large existing community, so an established audience is a competitive advantage over newer rivals.
principles.quote: when you have the social networking sites, you need a huge community. We have a good advantage, because we have had a community for years.

principles.text: Validate premium products by counting existing user demand before building them.
principles.quote: we have tens of requests a day for an application to tie into our database to update all of these files. We have a huge demand.

sources.title: How Hubert Thieblot grew Curse from a WoW add-on site into an MMOG portal (2007 interview)
sources.originalTitle: The Blessings of Curse: An Interview with Hubert Thieblot
sources.summary: A 2007 Escapist interview where Thieblot explains how Curse began as a personal tool for his guild and grew to 3.5M monthly uniques. He covers solving his own problem, listening to user feedback, going broad as a portal versus narrow databases, and diversifying beyond one game.

principles.text: Build the product to solve your own problem first; it can grow into a real business.
principles.quote: I did it largely for myself and my fellow guild members to make it easier to acquire WoW add-ons.

principles.text: Spot a disorganized, painful workflow in a hot new ecosystem and organize it.
principles.quote: Early in that game, I realized that finding and downloading add-ons was an extremely difficult and disorganized undertaking – so Curse-Gaming was born

principles.text: Respond to user feedback fast; small quick fixes show commitment to the user experience.
principles.quote: So, within a day, we cranked out a great-looking dark color scheme, which many of our users have adopted.

principles.text: Differentiate by being the single centralized destination rather than a point solution addressing one need.
principles.quote: Our goal is to provide a single, centralized location for MMOG gamers to turn to, regardless of what they need.

principles.text: Don't depend on one platform's success; expand to new games and markets and build developer relationships.
principles.quote: We’re doing so in various ways, including actively fostering relationships with developers, in order to expand our support for existing and upcoming titles.

principles.text: Surround a young founding team with experienced operators from your industry.
principles.quote: we’ve actively surrounded the founding team with successful professionals who have experience in the videogame industry.

sources.title: How Curse grew from a WoW add-on site to 23M monthly visitors
sources.originalTitle: Curse CEO Hubert Thieblot Wants To Create The Largest Gaming Media Property On The Web
sources.summary: Hubert Thieblot explains how Curse grew from a guild add-on tool he built alone into a 64-site gaming network. He covers hiring real gamers, using pro players as content producers, expanding across games, and monetizing via ads when costs outgrew his means.

principles.text: Start by solving your own community's problem; a useful internal tool can become a product for others.
principles.quote: The Website ended up being a useful tool, not just for members of the guild, but for other players as well.

principles.text: Hire true users of your product; their feedback is the best product signal.
principles.quote: When we are seeking new employees, it’s very important for us to hire real gamers.

principles.text: If your own staff uses your products, you will end up making good products.
principles.quote: If our staff uses our products, then we will make good products

principles.text: Expand beyond a niche once the market is too small: add new games, tools, and content types.
principles.quote: When we moved to the U.S., the market was too niche and we decided to grow and expand our offerings.

principles.text: When costs outgrow what you can cover, add ads as a revenue model to pay the bills.
principles.quote: My oldest brother suggested that ads could be a possible solution to generate profit and pay the bills.

principles.text: Use real experts as content contributors, not just as a branding play.
principles.quote: Real pro gamers are the best content contributors to create new guides.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hubert Thieblot, founder of Founders Inc and ex-Curse founder, makes the case for moving to SF and explains the campus, programs and investment model. He argues proximity to ambitious peers raises ambition, and that working side by side beats pitch decks as a way to invest.

chunks.heading: Why Hubert says founders should move to San Francisco
chunks.text:
- Hubert has spent the past year urging founders to move to SF and built Founders, Inc. to make that move easy.
- He started his first company, Curse, at 19. It grew from zero to 150+ employees and $50 million in revenue in its last year.
- He knew before starting that this would only be possible in San Francisco.
- Being there changed the company's trajectory. He became "way more ambitious" and "nothing felt impossible."
- Since selling Curse, his stated life mission is to help the next generation of founders find their path and their people, and to fund them.
- His 2026 goal: help 1,000 founders start their company in SF and give them what they need to hit the ground running, "exactly how I wish it happened for me."

chunks.heading: The campus model: three locations in San Francisco
chunks.text:
- **Fort Mason:** the first place invited founders visit. It is an always-on hub for building without distractions.
  - He says 90% of the experience is a daily cycle of building, learning and iterating alongside other founders on campus.
  - The team runs regular office hours and sessions with experienced founders who are anywhere from one to 100 steps ahead.
  - It also hosts public events for the wider SF community, such as hackathons, fireside chats and LAN parties.
- **The Garage:** the highest concentration of hardware founders in the city. It has four floors of industrial equipment and dedicated spaces for 30 teams.
- **A third, expanding space:** new space for the portfolio, with room for 100 founders.
- Hubert says the team runs the campus like a startup and keeps iterating as it grows.

chunks.heading: Hardware and physical AI conviction
chunks.text:
- 50% of Founders, Inc.'s 2025 investments were hardware.
- He envisions a future where physical AI and robotics are the biggest companies in the world.
- He says that for founders who believe the same, Founders, Inc. wants to be their "first and biggest supporter."
- Hardware teams are accepted in every program. In the Blueprint program, hardware and physical AI become the only focus for everyone on campus.

chunks.heading: How to get in and how investing works
chunks.text:
- The process is: apply online, get invited to the space, work closely together on accelerating growth, and invest if both sides feel it is a good fit.
- The campus runs 24/7. If you apply today, the team can contact you that night and you can be there the next day.
- He frames the evaluation as two-way: founders also get to judge whether Founders, Inc. is the right partner.
- If a founder felt real acceleration, Founders, Inc. finances the company.

chunks.heading: Programs that scale the intake
chunks.text:
- Four main programs run over the year, each bringing in hundreds of founders at once.
- Each is followed by a six-week cohort and ends with a demo day festival, where thousands of builders and investors come to see the work.
- In the off-season, 200 students fly out for the summer.
- A fourth program is coming that will bring together founders from all over the world.

chunks.heading: No pitch decks: judge founders by working together
chunks.text:
- Hubert says "we absolutely hate pitch decks." He never liked making them as a founder.
- His reasoning: building a company is about doing, not making a polished presentation.
- He argues the team learns far more about a founder's potential by working with them in person.

chunks.heading: What investment unlocks
chunks.text:
- After the first investment, the campus becomes fully unlocked for the founder.
- Portfolio benefits include:
  - Internal events exclusive to the portfolio.
  - Weekly accountability sessions.
  - More perks and credits.
  - A community platform for finding elite hires and co-founders, and for support with downstream investors.
- The Founders, Inc. team works hands-on with portfolio companies on product, media and go-to-market.
- His summary of the offer: a path to San Francisco, a community of other ambitious founders, and the intensity to win.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2010 CBS5 interview where Hubert Thieblot explains Curse, a platform for World of Warcraft and MMO players. He covers being a distribution platform for community-built tools, a two-channel revenue model of ads and subscriptions, and staffing with real gamers.

chunks.heading: Curse's scale and what it built (2010)
chunks.text:
- Hubert was CEO of Curse, Inc., a platform helping gamers succeed in massively multiplayer online games (MMOs). In his words: "helping Gamers succeed in this very complex virtual worlds" by providing "the right tools and information they need when they play the game."
- Scale in December 2010: about 6 million unique users and about 100 million page views per month.
- The Curse Client was one of the two biggest projects. It organizes players' game files and add-ons, and about 1.2 million people were using it actively.
- Games covered: World of Warcraft, Warhammer Online, Age of Conan, Aion and Diablo 3.

chunks.heading: Distribution platform instead of building every tool
chunks.text:
- Curse did not build the add-ons itself. The community of developers did.
- Curse acted as the distribution platform for small applications that players install and use while playing. Hubert compared it to the iPhone App Store.
- Reach: about 10,000 applications and more than 3,000 active developers.
- Curse's own part was the surrounding infrastructure: the website, forums, and databases of all the quests, weapons and monsters.
- Takeaway from his approach: let a community of creators supply the supply side, and own distribution and the information layer around it.

chunks.heading: Two revenue channels: advertising and premium subscriptions
chunks.text:
- **Advertising** was the first channel. It is why Curse moved operations to the US: about 45% of its traffic was American, so the sales team had to be there.
- **Premium subscriptions** were the second. Users could subscribe monthly or yearly to get additional features on the site.
- Lesson in his reasoning: he placed the sales team where the traffic and advertisers were, not where the company started.

chunks.heading: Staying relevant in a fast-changing industry
chunks.text:
- Hubert says gaming evolves constantly. What Curse was doing four years earlier "would be completely nearly useless" in 2010.
- His answer was to play all the games himself: "it's really important to play all the games to know what's going on."
- He hired a team that "really gets it." Every employee plays MMOs and has high industry experience.
- The principle: build for gamers with gamers. The team members are users of the product, so they know exactly what other players want and need.

chunks.heading: Roadmap and infrastructure
chunks.text:
- Two big projects in the works: continuing development of the Curse Client, and a large social networking product.
- Infrastructure: Curse ran on a bit more than 25 servers, provided free through Microsoft's BizSpark startup program.
- Beyond free hosting, BizSpark gave easy access to Microsoft. Curse could talk directly to Microsoft developers to solve scalability problems.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hubert Thieblot explains how Curse built a free voice and overlay app for League of Legends by fixing the questions players keep asking in chat. He covers handling publisher risk through transparency, scaling cheaply with better compression, delaying monetization to win 100M PC gamers, and shifting from content to technology platforms.

chunks.heading: Curse's mission: fix gaming communication, free, and own the platform layer
chunks.text:
Hubert (CEO of Curse, ~120 employees, about 70% of whom play League of Legends) frames Curse Voice as a quality-of-life fix for a clear problem. His method: look at what players ask over and over in chat and remove the friction.
- The most repeated questions were "when is the old app up", "when is dragon" and "when is baron". He says these stop people from actually playing, so Curse fixed them.
- He says Curse was founded in World of Warcraft 9 years ago on the same approach: "we looked at problem and we looked at things that just don't make sense."
- Goal: improve quality of life and communication, not build "the ultimate timer application that does everything for you." Red and blue buff timers are "a no-brainer" later, but "we're not going to time every single thing on the map."

chunks.heading: Why old voice tools don't fit the new game type
chunks.text:
Hubert argues voice software failed to keep up with how games changed.
- Six or seven years ago, in WoW and other MMOs, you played with people you knew, in a guild, so Ventrilo, TeamSpeak and Skype worked as long-term relationship tools.
- League of Legends and other MOBAs push you to play with strangers, with "one or two minutes to talk before a game". He says the old tools don't apply, and the same goes for World of Tanks and Minecraft.
- Positioning: a very easy way to chat with people. No friend list needed; share a link and they join. Friend lists, IM and chat rooms come later (the TeamSpeak-style "hang out in a room" use case within a couple of months).
- He considers TeamSpeak and Ventrilo "the old era of MMO" and not relevant long term.
- Skype critique: it became cluttered from supporting mobile and every platform, and it is peer-to-peer, so hosting a call makes your PC work hard (FPS and RAM complaints). Curse is not peer-to-peer, and he says players cannot get each other's IP through it.

chunks.heading: Technical choices and prioritizing stability
chunks.text:
- V1 took about 9 months of work. It uses the latest codec and compresses "about four to five times more than on Skype", so bandwidth use is tiny.
- Servers are distributed worldwide (Taiwan, Australia, Brazil, eastern and western Europe, US east and west coast) and capacity can be raised in a region "in just a matter of seconds". Everything runs on the cloud.
- China is excluded because it already has good gamer communication apps.
- Skype is stuck on an old codec because changing it breaks every client until updated across many platforms. Curse, focused on PC, can ship better audio.
- Top priority is stability: "We don't want to crash your game. We don't want to impact your FPS." Works for 99% of users; about 1% with special drivers or graphics cards have issues, and some have headset compatibility bugs. The team was working about 14 hours a day.
- A Mac developer was hired; Mac would take a couple of months, VoIP first, overlay after.

chunks.heading: Beta rollout and scarcity-driven demand
chunks.text:
- Beta grew from 0 to 7,000 to 40,000 users, then close to half a million active users, with another million who visited the site without access.
- A jump in the beta pool from 7,000 to about 50,000 about 10 days earlier raised awareness and caused the controversy.
- He says the controversy is partly because the app wasn't open yet: "if you don't have something that other people have, the interaction is always going to be a bit weird."
- Millions of accounts had registered on the website for Curse Voice. He says Curse has to represent what the community wants, and that most people want the timers.

chunks.heading: Handling the publisher relationship and controversy
chunks.text:
Hubert's approach with Riot, whose rules and bans could affect the product:
- Be transparent early. Curse told Riot in February what it was doing and why, about three months into beta, rather than surprising them.
- Riot's legitimate concerns were moderation, matching random players in voice, abuse, and add-ons giving a competitive advantage or cheating. He says Curse shares those concerns.
- He expects Riot to publish a policy and believes the timers will be fine. He would not ship something the publisher is definitely against, and he would not be surprised if Riot built timers into the game.
- Commitments: work with Riot on moderation, ban people if needed, and adopt Riot's best practices on toxicity. He notes a voice account carries lower stakes than a game account, so mechanics must be designed accordingly.
- Self-positioning: "We're here to support everyone, the players, the game companies also." He says Curse understands both players and publishers and can be "a great middleman." He admits he can't predict whether Riot may later object to the in-client integration.

chunks.heading: Free product and monetization philosophy
chunks.text:
- Communication and any game integration "will always be free."
- Planned experiments (no fixed plan or timeline): Asian-style communication-platform monetization such as special emoticons and premium memberships for nice-to-have features, plus other real-time services, since every user is logged in and ready to interact.
- "Monetization is not my worry." Number one objective: about 100 million hardcore PC gamers outside China, all on the voice platform.
- Next games under consideration: Hearthstone, World of Tanks or Diablo.

chunks.heading: Company strategy: from content to technology platforms
chunks.text:
- Core business then was the website network: about 1.1 billion page views a month and 43 to 44 million users the previous month.
- Other platform bets: a YouTube program helping creators monetize and get known, and the voice client.
- His reasoning for moving to technology: web growth is limited without new big games, and "content has more local than technology". Curse built an app in 9 months that could launch worldwide.
- Focus is PC and Mac as open platforms. He cites a study that PC gaming had overtaken console as a worldwide market, helped by mobile games expanding the pool of players with low-spec PCs. He sees enough opportunity there that he doesn't expect to move to other platforms for a long time.
- He expects add-on ecosystems like WoW's not to repeat in League, since it's a simpler game where, for example, a DPS meter would be pointless.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a comedic interview, Hubert Thieblot explains how he writes early checks on vibe, backing ambitious, fast-moving technical founders instead of judging the idea. He also shares founder advice: pick the hardest problem you care about, and don't hire a compliance officer too early.

chunks.heading: How Hubert decides on $150K checks: vibes, ambition and technical depth
chunks.text:
- Hubert says he "mostly invest[s] on vibe" when writing early checks. The example is a roughly $150,000 check to two founders aged 17 and 18, decided right after a same-day conversation.
- The pair had built robots, machine learning algorithms and many other projects. Hubert was impressed by what they had done for their age.
- He is not concerned with the idea: "I actually don't care too much about the idea." He asks founders for the idea mainly to learn how ambitious they are.
- He also checks whether they are good people and team players, and he prefers to find them by looking around the internet for people with ideas.

chunks.heading: What Hubert screens for in founders
chunks.text:
- **Ambition.** He asks whether you are ambitious.
- **Speed and resourcefulness.** He asks whether you will "move really fast and find ways to unblock yourself."
- **Technical ability.** He asks whether you can build a really hard product or company.
- **Focus area.** The firm generally tends to focus on emerging technology such as AI and robotics.

chunks.heading: The hangar: a 42,000 sq ft space for founders
chunks.text:
- The idea is "a hangar for founders": a physical place where people gather, start their journey and create things.
- Founders are surrounded by other very fast movers and ambitious people.
- Hubert confirms the 42,000 sq ft space as the home for the founders he backs.

chunks.heading: Why Europe held founders back, and why San Francisco felt different
chunks.text:
- Hubert started the company in December 2004 in Heidelberg, Germany, and later moved it to the US.
- He says many VCs had a "virus" of giving reasons you can't do something: you're too young, you have no degrees. He did not finish high school.
- When he landed in San Francisco, the attitude was the opposite: "why can you not do that?"
- His view is that Europe needs to take more risk, go faster and "break some regulation."
- He says that in venture you have to go fast, because if you go slow your competition will kill you.
- He allows that some worries about how fast AI is moving, such as job displacement, "can be legitimate."

chunks.heading: Curse: what he built and what it taught him
chunks.text:
- Curse was a modding platform. In games like World of Warcraft or Minecraft, users could install mods to change parts of the game or the user interface.
- It was a 12-plus year journey before the company was acquired. He calls it "life-changing."
- He says there were lots of failures and some successes, and he had to learn how to create a company along the way.
- He credits some luck too: "I think I got lucky also."

chunks.heading: Advice for young founders
chunks.text:
1. **Don't hire a compliance officer too early.** He says: "Do not hire a compliance officer before you have something that needs a compliance officer." He suggests it can wait until roughly a month after you start.
2. **Dream the biggest you can and take on the hardest problem you actually care about.** It is obvious when people work on random things they don't care about.
3. **Care, or you will quit.** Founders who don't care about the problem will mostly give up the first time it gets really hard, so he values grit.
4. **Win with ethics.** He says winning should come "with some ethics and beliefs."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hubert Thieblot explains why Curse moved HQ from San Francisco to Huntsville. Hiring was the biggest growth constraint, and competing with well-funded Bay Area companies for talent was not a game worth playing. He walks through the five criteria used to pick a city and the logic of being a big fish in a smaller, rising market.

chunks.heading: Why Curse moved its HQ from San Francisco to Huntsville, Alabama
chunks.text: In September 2014, as CEO of the online game portal Curse Inc., Hubert explained why Curse relocated its headquarters from San Francisco to Huntsville, Alabama. The company's biggest challenge was growing the team fast enough to keep up with the company. He decided Curse couldn't "slug it out" for talent against the very large, very well-funded companies in San Francisco, so the company would "make its own path" and break from the Silicon Valley stereotype.

chunks.heading: Five criteria for choosing where to build a company
chunks.text:
Hubert's team looked at more than 10 US cities. The factors, in order:

1. Talent pool
2. Work-life balance
3. Business environment
4. Cost efficiency
5. Potential

- **Talent pool comes first.** Moving somewhere without finding talented employees makes no sense.
- **The tech scene must be strong but not saturated.** If competition is too heavy, hiring becomes prohibitively expensive or so slow that it slows down production.
- **Match the place to the team.** Curse's staff is younger, active and educated, so the location had to appeal to and reflect that demographic.
- **Optimize for a sustainable work experience.** He wants happy employees and a lifestyle the location supports.

chunks.heading: Cost efficiency means value, not just savings
chunks.text:
Hubert says the key "isn't to simply save," because Curse could put a team in another country for that. The goal was to "get the most bang for our buck" and build an infrastructure in a location that would be efficient.

On Huntsville's economics, he said: "Huntsville is the perfect location from a cost standpoint. It feels a little bit like Austin, Texas, about 10 years ago, when it started on its way up. Corporate real estate is inexpensive, the cost of talent is reasonable and housing for our staff is incredibly affordable."

chunks.heading: Be a big fish in an emerging market, not a drop in the bucket
chunks.text:
- Hubert did not want Curse to be only "a drop in the bucket in a larger market," even as a fast-growing, successful startup.
- He chose not to follow the herd to the trendy corporate location. Curse would "rather blaze a trail toward an up and coming community" and help shape its evolution from the start.
- The result in Huntsville: a "small fish-big pond" mentality no longer applied, and the company felt wanted.
- Curse's Huntsville presence was set to grow from about 20 to about 40 people as the HQ relocation completed.

chunks.heading: Talent outcome in Huntsville
chunks.text:
- Huntsville's talent pool comes largely from the aerospace industry and NASA (Marshall Space Flight Center). Hubert rated the level of expertise and education as very good.
- Curse was filling significantly more positions locally than it expected.
- Social and entertainment options and a thriving business community kept staff comfortable and happy.

chunks.heading: Working with local government and building a "Silicon South"
chunks.text:
- Hubert credits the Huntsville Chamber of Commerce, Downtown Huntsville, the City of Huntsville and the Alabama Commerce Department with making significant resources available and easing the transition.
- He wanted a location that "would work for other companies similar to ours," reasoning that if Curse met its own criteria there, others would follow. He saw companies trending away from the high cost and difficult recruiting of established markets.
- Curse's ambition was to be part of establishing a "Silicon South" in Alabama.
- Tactics to promote the hub: talk to other companies and the venture capital community in the gaming space and tell the Huntsville story, and bring teams down to see the nightlife, activities and environment firsthand. Hubert reports the response is consistently positive.

chunks.heading: Context at the time of the move
chunks.text:
- Hubert described Curse as having several rapidly growing products, newly secured funding to reach "the next level," and technical infrastructure that would scale for some time.
- He framed hiring capacity, not product or funding, as the main constraint on growth, and treated location as a hiring strategy.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hubert Thieblot explains how Curse started as a guild website and WoW add-on database, grew by being the first, biggest and best in its niche, then added social tools years later. He covers moving to San Francisco, raising a $5M Series A, and expanding toward publishers and premium subscriptions.

chunks.heading: Curse began as a World of Warcraft add-on database built to solve his own guild's problem
chunks.text:
- In 2005 Hubert managed a hardcore MMO guild called Curse (Dark Age of Camelot, World of Warcraft, some Korean games).
- During the WoW alpha, getting information on add-ons and updates from the official forums was "a complete mess." So he built a database.
- It drew a lot of traffic and attention, and that is when he turned Curse into a business.
- His original goal was modest: get attention for his guild and "live off of advertising." He says he "would never have expected it to be this big, two years later."
- He built it without any social network. Social features were only added about six months before the interview. He uses Facebook and MySpace and watches what they do, but did not copy them.

chunks.heading: The add-on traffic engine: be first, biggest and best at a niche utility
chunks.text:
- Early traffic came from the add-on section. WoW add-ons let players customize health bars, quest display and more, which "completely changes the user experience."
- Hubert credits the draw to being "the first, the biggest and the best on the net." He says Curse "surfed on that wave" for about two and a half years.
- By August 2007 the site had 3.5 million uniques (up from 1.5 million) and 80 to 100 million page views. Revenue grew in 2006.
- Early monetization was advertising: Google AdSense and other ad networks, with his brother joining as co-founder in late 2005.
- Real development (database, Wiki, forums, social networking) only began about a year before the interview.

chunks.heading: Product evolution: from a utility to a full community portal
chunks.text:
- Version 2 was "really just an improved version 1." Version 3 (December 2006) was a "fully Web 2.0 approach to business."
- The team grew from 5 to 20 and the site went through several redesigns in about a year.
- Added tools: game databases, game-specific Wikis, forums, user-submitted videos, social networking.
- He argues Curse is not an editorial company. Its developers have played MMOs for nearly a decade, so they build from inside the user's experience rather than writing articles.
- Planned features: a guild package ("a full package for a guild, including all their needs"), plus a desktop application tied to the database that updates add-on files.

chunks.heading: Why a premium subscription: demand he already saw
chunks.text:
- Hubert planned a monthly premium subscription to compete with GameSpot, FilePlanet and IGN, tying together the social network, add-ons and downloads.
- Evidence of demand: "tens of requests a day" for an application that ties into the database to update add-on files.
- He saw "a few big gaps of service that MMO gamers need covered" by existing sites.

chunks.heading: Competing with incumbents: community scale is the moat for social features
chunks.text:
- Targets for direct competition included IGN, GameSpot and other large game sites.
- On niche social competitors such as Guild Cafe: "when you have the social networking sites, you need a huge community. We have a good advantage, because we have had a community for years."
- On the size of the opportunity: players come and go from games, and no network tracks "people you played with a year ago, or two years ago." Building that history takes a lot of players, and he believes Curse is best placed to do it.
- Hubert views Asian MMOs as a gap. Most have no official website or a nearly non-existent one, so there is nowhere for the community to share advice, videos and achievements. Curse wants to be that place. He cites Lineage II, which still had many subscribers with little coverage.

chunks.heading: Becoming a service company for developers and publishers
chunks.text:
- Curse was already in the content programs for most big MMOs: interviewing developers and publishers, getting exclusive assets, running contests.
- Publishers get value because Curse supports their game and makes users play more. They also buy advertising on the site.
- Next step: building official game sites for publishers and developers. He wants Curse to position itself as "a service company" that applies what it learned building a multi-service site.
- He was also building "a huge sales force," saying "making money is a huge part of Curse, and it's what we do everyday."
- He wants to serve developers and publishers while serving the community "in the maximum possible way."

chunks.heading: Relocation and funding
chunks.text:
- Moves: France to Germany (to add people), then San Francisco. He says Paris was not the place to scale.
- Reason for San Francisco: most big game-site players are in the US and it is the hub of Web 2.0 companies. He did not want to be a copycat bringing a US concept to Europe. He wanted to compete head-on with IGN and GameSpot, and found developers and media management talent there.
- Funding: an $800K angel round in December 2006, then a $5 million Series A in July 2007 from a French VC firm. He found US opportunities more plentiful than European ones. He says raising "was not hard," and the French round came mostly through strong connections there.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2007 Escapist interview where Thieblot explains how Curse began as a personal tool for his guild and grew to 3.5M monthly uniques. He covers solving his own problem, listening to user feedback, going broad as a portal versus narrow databases, and diversifying beyond one game.

chunks.heading: Curse's origin as a player-built tool
chunks.text:
- Hubert started Curse as an MMOG guild in early 2001, playing smaller Korean MMOGs and *Dark Age of Camelot*, where the guild gained some notoriety.
- *World of Warcraft* turned the guild into a service. He found that locating and downloading add-ons was "extremely difficult and disorganized", so he built Curse-Gaming to fix it.
- He built it "largely for myself and my fellow guild members". He never expected it to be "wildly successful".
- The add-on downloads database made it one of the most visited third-party WoW sites quickly.
- Lesson he draws: solving his own annoying problem as a player became a business, turning "my passion into a business".

chunks.heading: Growth and team scaling (2005 to 2007)
chunks.text:
- Curse launched in 2005. By August 2007 it had over 3.5 million monthly unique visitors.
- Staff had quadrupled and traffic "grown rapidly" over those two years.
- He was young, so he deliberately surrounded the founding team with experienced professionals from the videogame industry.
- The company had been through several redesigns (V3, then V4) before the Curse.com relaunch.
- A Series-A round was raised to support every aspect of the business and the vision of innovating for the community. He hired technical and moderation staff ahead of the expanded scope.

chunks.heading: Expanding from one tool to a portal
chunks.text:
- V4 moved Curse from an add-on download site to a social and encyclopedic portal: social networking, wikis (such as WoWWiki), in-game databases for *Vanguard* and *WoW*, blogs, forums, MyCurse and the Curse Client.
- He admits the wider scope is "a great challenge" but says it "translates into many opportunities".
- V4 had been in the works a long time: "We planted many of the seeds for the V4 changes in V3."
- He calls V4 "just a first step" and refuses to commit to a "V5" label. The team is always building new features "with our users in mind".

chunks.heading: Positioning against competitors
chunks.text:
- Competitors named: Thottbot, Allakhazam, Wowhead (all owned by The Zam Network, an IGE spin-off).
- His view: they built good WoW item and quest databases but are not portals. They "only address one aspect of an MMOG gamer's needs", which he says brings no value to the community or to game developers.
- Curse's goal is "a single, centralized location" for MMOG gamers: add-ons, blogs, forums, databases, wikis or nearly anything else.
- Differentiation is breadth plus owning the whole player workflow, not winning a single feature race.

chunks.heading: Reducing dependence on one game
chunks.text:
- WoW drove much of Curse's traffic. He acknowledges the whole MMOG industry benefited from Blizzard's success.
- Plan to broaden: keep leadership as the WoW portal while supporting all MMOGs.
- Tactics: build relationships with game developers to support existing and upcoming titles; expand into free-to-play and item-based games.
- Bet: Asian-market games would reach the U.S. the following year, and a mainstream console MMOG would eventually lift the whole industry. Curse intended to be there for it.

chunks.heading: Listening to the community
chunks.text:
- User feedback is treated as a core input. Users share it actively, both positive and negative.
- Example: after V4 launched with a light color scheme, several users disliked it versus earlier dark versions. Within a day the team "cranked out" a dark color scheme, which many adopted.
- He frames this as small in design terms but proof of the commitment to user experience.
- The team are gamers themselves. They still play together and evaluate upcoming releases to decide how to serve each community. He says this understanding of the industry "has a very important impact on how we innovate".
- He used to play 14-hour days; running and growing Curse now takes the same time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hubert Thieblot explains how Curse grew from a guild add-on tool he built alone into a 64-site gaming network. He covers hiring real gamers, using pro players as content producers, expanding across games, and monetizing via ads when costs outgrew his means.

chunks.heading: Starting Curse from a World of Warcraft guild site
chunks.text:
- Hubert did not start Curse to make money. He says he "started Curse, not as a way to make money, but as a venture to help the community."
- Curse was the name of his World of Warcraft guild, one of the strongest in the European PvE scene, with many EU-first kills.
- The guild needed a site to organize and share add-ons, so he built Curse-Gaming.com. It turned out to be useful to players outside the guild too.
- His first taste of eSports came from that guild, which briefly played in professional tournaments. His older brother was a pro Counter-Strike gamer who competed in Korea.

chunks.heading: Early growth: from solo founder to ads, then funding
chunks.text:
- At first Curse only served WoW add-ons. After moving to the U.S., Hubert found that market "too niche" and widened it.
- Expansion meant new games plus news, tips and wikis for gamers.
- At the start he was the only employee and handled servers, design and everything else.
- The site outgrew what he could manage alone and he couldn't cover its costs. His oldest brother suggested ads as a way to pay the bills, and then became the first employee.
- The company later moved to Germany and a third person helped with web development. After that they went looking for funding, and San Francisco seemed the right place to find it.
- Scale as of 2012:
  - More than 64 sites.
  - Staff grew from 3 in 2007 to over 75 full-time plus over 50 contractors or part-time workers.
  - Reach grew from nothing to over 23 million visitors a month.

chunks.heading: Product strategy: hire real gamers and build tools for passionate players
chunks.text:
- Curse's strategy has always been to provide "the best tools, resources and information for passionate gamers."
- Hubert pays close attention to hiring and insists on real gamers. A team with true passion for gaming is the best way to build the best tools.
- His reasoning: "There is no better feedback than that which we receive from our own employees. If our staff uses our products, then we will make good products."

chunks.heading: Expansion tactics: new games, new formats, and an owned pro team
chunks.text:
- Curse watches for new games it can serve with the best content for its audience.
- It follows how people consume information, which is why it also pushed into YouTube and video.
- The pro team is a content engine, not a branding play. It feeds LoLPro.com, and Hubert says "Real pro gamers are the best content contributors to create new guides. They know the best tips and ways to play each of the Champions."
- In 2011 Curse bought Team Curse when League of Legends was becoming prominent in pro gaming.
- Curse owned a pair of League of Legends teams, in Europe and the U.S., with Team Curse Houses in Los Angeles and Berlin. It livestreams from those houses to connect gamers with pros.

chunks.heading: Livestreaming: a regular schedule
chunks.text:
- Hubert's livestreaming priority is "a regularly scheduled program."
- His reasoning: "People want to follow their favorite streamers and they don't know at what time to tune in. Scheduled programing will satisfy the audience's needs."

chunks.heading: Reading eSports titles: why League of Legends works and StarCraft II doesn't
chunks.text:
- Riot's success with League of Legends: "a good game that is fun to watch and play," with "a low level of entry, but a high range to mastery," which builds a bigger audience willing to invest time.
- Riot's Finals at USC filled an arena, which he takes as evidence of the size of the North American eSports audience. The large cash prizes also helped draw attention.
- StarCraft II: he calls it "really saturated" and sees no bright future in North American eSports. It is less fun to watch than League of Legends, and hard to play at the beginning, which discourages players and fans.
- Halo 4 and Call of Duty: Black Ops II: their new spectator mode makes it easier to attract viewers and fans.

chunks.heading: Brand and long-term vision
chunks.text:
- Curse was not well known to the mainstream. Hubert's plan to build the brand is to provide resources for more and more games, which widens the market and attracts more people.
- On core gamers, he says they "aren't going away" and may even grow in number as the industry goes mainstream.
- His five-year goal for Curse: "The largest gaming media property on the Web."

My personal magical SF story is from early 2009, when an angel investor quite literally saved my company.

I needed sales advice to boost revenue fast, so I emailed a bunch of sales VPs I respected. One replied.

She met with me at the W downtown and we talked for a few hours, she was super helpful and open, offered to make intros to potential clients and sales reps. 

In the middle she picks up her phone, and asked, “Do you mind if my boyfriend joins? He loves your product.”
I said, yeah! He had sold his company to google a few years back. 

He was super curious about my whole story and i told him about the cash problem and what I was going to do to solve growth. He was a gamer himself so he understood our product very well and had some good ideas. I told him it was hard to find investors for a bridge, everyone was worried it wouldn’t be enough for the company to make it. We had gone from everyone is investing in startups to no one. The next day he wrote me a 200K check as a loan that could convert to equity. I had been a total stranger to him 24 hours earlier. He told me to use that momentum to get others. Within two days I had 600K.

Six months later, I raised a Series A, and our growth had picked up again.

This would not have happened anywhere else in the world.

As a founder, I never really understood how VC funds work and how partners make money so here is a simple explanation: 

👥 Who does what

GPs (General Partners), run the fund + make final decisions. They are also expected to invest in the fund, at least a few %. 
Principals, source deals, diligence, sometimes lead
Analysts/Associates, research, sourcing, DM anyone going viral on X/LinkedIn
LPs (Limited Partners) — the fund’s investors: pensions, endowments, family offices, wealthy individuals

👉 Small funds = 1–3 decision makers → fast yes/no
👉 Big funds = partner meetings + investment committees → multi-week process
➡️ Always know who can actually say YES and how long it will take. 

⸻

💰 How GPs make money

1️⃣ Management fees
~2% of total raised by the fund per year (≈20% over 10 years)
• Large funds = gps can make millions a year
• Small/mid size funds = 50k-200k a year max 

2️⃣ Carry (profit share)
After LPs get their money back, GPs usually take 20% of profits
This is the wealth engine especially for smaller funds. 

⸻

📈 Carry example

Fund invests $1M at $10M valuation
→ starts at 10%
→ diluted to ~5%
Exit = $10B

Math:
Fund receives: $500M
Profit: $499M
Carry (20%): $99.8M to GPs

If it’s a $50M fund:
✔ Fund returns 10×
✔ GPs take ~$100M in carry

One winner can define a fund

⸻

🧪 Fundraising grind
GPs raise new funds every 2–3 years
Takes 6+ months, constant pitching, tons of rejection
Empathy moment: VCs are fundraising too and it’s way more brutal than raising for you startup.  Usually hundreds of meetings over 1 year, all over the world. 

⸻

🧾 Back office 
Running a fund costs $1M-2M over its life:
• legal
• audit/tax
• compliance
• admin + reporting
Big funds spend millions more
AngelList/Carta make it cheaper

⸻

⏳ Fund timeline
Most funds = 10 years but can be extended every year 
Years 1–3: investment period 
Years 4–10: support + return capital
As funds age, pressure builds to exit companies

Think of your startup like pushing a boulder on a steep mountain:

Stage 1: The Sisyphus Phase

You’re at the bottom, pushing uphill. It takes Herculean effort just to move an inch. The second you stop pushing (marketing, pushing new features), the boulder rolls back to zero. No momentum.

Stage 2: The Plateau

You’ve pushed it onto a flat ledge. If you stop pushing, it doesn’t roll back completely, but it doesn’t move forward either much.  This is where most founders get stuck. In general, you get stuck here here without great retention and marketing you can repeat. They think this is PMF. It isn't.

Stage 3: The Tipping Point

Suddenly, the boulder starts moving without you. You see signups from a random user post that went viral. You can’t pinpoint where 200 new users came from. You get emails out of no where of serious customers that wants to buy your service. The market is finally pulling the product out of you.

Stage 4: The Avalanche

The charts go vertical. You have made it to the other side.  Retention is so high that growth just happens. Stability breaks because you’re scaling faster than you can code and build systems in your company. You have unlimited capital and crisis to manage. You need to hire and fast. All this holdco hype is nonsense. These $1–2M/year revenue apps aren’t going to cut it. How do I know? I built one that generated $50M+ in revenue.

For holdcos to work:
•You need to pursue decently large opportunities. If something can’t generate $10M+ in annual revenue, don’t bother.
•You need long-term, substantial cash flow businesses. Most AI wrapper apps are unlikely to achieve this due to constant disruption from technological advancements.
•Building many apps in parallel doesn’t work. Focus on one large app first, then expand to other apps only when growth opportunities for the initial app stall.
•VC money is unlikely to be effective, except for early-stage investors or if you can scale to $100M+ in revenue with significant EBITDA. You gotta be super capital efficient. Every dollar count.
